questions.q: Where is every run of WorkOrderETL.dtsx logged, whether triggered by the Agent job or run manually?
options: In a text file on the developer's local machine
Only inside the Power BI Service
Inside the SSISDB catalog itself, visible in SSMS under Integration Services Catalogs
Nowhere — SSIS package runs are not logged by default
questions.explain: SSISDB logs every execution of a deployed package regardless of what triggered it, which is exactly why the catalog is the first place to check.

questions.q: Which SSISDB report would you check to see exactly what parameter values a specific past run of WorkOrderETL used?
options: All Executions
Active Operations
Job Activity Monitor
Refresh history
questions.explain: All Executions lets you pick any date range and inspect the exact parameter values a given run used — Active Operations only shows what's running right now.

questions.q: What does SQL Server Agent's View History show for the WorkOrderETL job?
options: Only the next scheduled run time
The T-SQL source code of the SSIS package
The Power BI dataset's refresh schedule
Every past run of the job, its outcome, and per-step detail
questions.explain: View History (right-click the job in SQL Server Agent) is the record of every past run and its outcome, step by step.

questions.q: What does Power BI's refresh history show for a semantic model?
options: The SQL Server Agent job that populated the warehouse
Status, duration, and the exact error message for every scheduled refresh attempt
The list of workspace members
The .pbix file's original publish date only
questions.explain: Refresh history is a grid of every refresh attempt with its status, duration, and error message when one fails — the Power BI-side equivalent of checking All Executions in SSISDB.

questions.q: Why does this lesson describe day-to-day monitoring as checking three separate places — the SSIS catalog, SQL Server Agent, and Power BI's refresh history — rather than one unified dashboard?
options: Each tool logs its own half of the pipeline, and a BI developer's basic operational check means knowing where to look in each one, not assuming a single tool reports on all of them
Only Power BI actually logs anything useful
SQL Server Agent and SSISDB always show identical information
A unified monitoring dashboard is required before any of this pipeline can be trusted
questions.explain: This is deliberately practical, BI-developer-scoped monitoring — knowing which of the three tools' own built-in history to check, not standing up a separate observability platform.
